edbDesc: A process, or technique to reduce wear of one or both surfaces in close proximity, and moving relative to each other, by interposing a substance (lubricant) between the surfaces to carry or to help carry the load (pressure generated) between the opposing surfaces. The interposed lubricant film can be a solid, (e.g. graphite) a solid/liquid dispersion, a liquid, a liquid-liquid dispersion (a grease) or, exceptionally, a gas.
title: Lubrication
description: A spinning shaft drags oil into the narrowing gap of its bearing and builds enough pressure to float on it, so metal never touches metal. Beauchamp Tower discovered that pressure in 1883 when oil spurted from a hole drilled in a railway-axle bearing, and Osborne Reynolds explained it in 1886.
effect: a moving surface drags oil into a wedge-shaped gap and floats on it
usedIn: Journal bearings in car engines and turbines
Michell thrust bearings on ship propeller shafts
strength: An oil film thinner than a hair can carry tens of atmospheres of pressure and cuts friction to about a thousandth of the load.
pickWhy: Borderline: Judgment call: 'lubrication' is a general practice (e1), but the oil-wedge effect Tower found is specific and powerful; kept under the broad name, framed as hydrodynamic lubrication.
